tools.name: action-button
tools.description: Press the iPhone or iPad Action Button once. The press is dispatched without activating the session app and nothing is re-observed afterwards, so the app keeps the state the press found. What the system does with the press is not observed by this command: Simulators run no Shortcuts or App Intents, so delivery to an assigned Shortcut is verifiable only on a physical iPhone. A model with no Action Button refuses with UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION, error.details.reason hardware_control_unavailable and dispatched: no. Times out after 90s.

tools.name: alert
tools.description: Inspect, wait for, accept, or dismiss a platform alert. The get action reads alert content; accept and dismiss change the active alert state. Each iOS XCTest execution activates once, then only observes. Apple XCTest and Limrun iOS choose recognized English labels by preference (Allow While Using App before Allow Once); on iOS simulators, including Limrun, the runner also recognizes the device's preferred languages' wording of those labels from the OS permission-prompt strings, on any alert; equal-ranked choices and unknown labels refuse, including a lone unknown button. Open, Done, and Confirm… accept; Keep Browsing, Deny, and Skip dismiss. On the Apple XCUITest runner, dismiss taps only a recognized decline label (Cancel, Don't Allow, Ask App Not to Track, and similar) or the close element of a popover whose accessibility marker reads exactly "dismiss popup"; when no button fits the action, accept and dismiss answer ALERT_BUTTON_NOT_FOUND having tapped nothing. The get action exposes labels for explicit button targeting. A get result with status none reports no alert. An alert-not-found refusal means no alert was found and no button was pressed. An alert-wait-timeout means no actionable alert resolved within the wait window. A refusal with dispatched: no means no button was activated. After a press, an unconfirmed outcome leaves the resulting alert state unknown. Times out after 90s.

tools.name: back
tools.description: Navigate back in the app or through system navigation. The in-app mode targets the app navigation stack; system targets platform back behavior. On iOS both modes press the navigation bar system back button (identifier BackButton) only when exactly one hittable one is found in a readable accessibility tree, and succeed only when the number of navigation bars, the number of back buttons, or a back button title then changes (a bar title or a moved back button alone never counts, so a pop that keeps the same back button title and bar count reports back_swipe_unverified); with no such button, two candidates, or an unreadable tree, they swipe from the left edge instead (on an iPad whose app window cannot be resolved, only while the app fills the screen) and succeed only when the app screen changes. Reason back_swipe_no_change: the swipe was sent and the screen did not change; a visible back or close control is an alternative. Reason back_swipe_unverified: the button was pressed but the navigation bar's back buttons did not change within 1 s or on one more read after it, or the swipe may or may not have navigated, because the screen kept changing before it or could not be sampled after it; the resulting screen is unconfirmed. Reason back_swipe_not_dispatched, or a screen that cannot be sampled before the swipe, means nothing was sent. An app with a left-edge drawer may open the drawer instead. A visible back or close control can be targeted directly by its ref. Times out after 90s; a caller-supplied budget extends it.

tools.name: batch
tools.description: Execute multiple commands in one daemon request. Use it for a known multi-step walk, such as press A, press B, back, instead of one tool call per step. steps is an array of {command, input} objects; input takes the same arguments as that command's own tool (ref, selector, or x and y for targets; settle: true for the settled diff). Steps run serially in one session; onError: "stop" halts at the first failing step, and the result reports the steps that ran. The daemon stops the whole batch after 60 seconds; split longer walks. Example steps, in order (refs such as @e12 come from the last snapshot or settled diff): {"command":"press","input":{"ref":"@e12","settle":true}}, {"command":"press","input":{"selector":"label=Settings","settle":true}}, {"command":"fill","input":{"selector":"id=\"field-email\"","text":"qa@example.com"}}, {"command":"scroll","input":{"direction":"down","until":"label=Privacy","settle":true}}, {"command":"back","input":{"settle":true}}, {"command":"wait","input":{"kind":"text","text":"Saved"}}, {"command":"snapshot","input":{"interactiveOnly":true}}. Times out after 90s.

Success reports dispatch only; settle returns the resulting UI diff and verify returns cheap post-action evidence. A ref or selector target is re-checked for motion before dispatch when the session's previous action just animated the screen, and is dispatched at its resting position; one that has not stopped refuses with target_still_moving rather than acting where it was. With settle, continue from the returned diff. Copy refs exactly, including any ~sN suffix. Times out after 90s; a caller-supplied budget extends it.

tools.name: close
tools.description: Close the named app, or close the active session app when app is omitted. The shutdown option also stops the session simulator or emulator where supported; close alone never stops the device. Android ADB close fails with android-app-close-timeout if the app stays foreground past 2s, a killed process does not exit within 10s, or a new process runs past 2s; a relaunching open accepts that new process. It fails with android-process-probe-unavailable when adb pidof cannot list the app processes; if that happens before the force-stop, the app keeps running. If close cannot confirm its cleanup on a session that holds a device claim, the session and its claim stay. A repeated close retries cleanup with the same options, except that save-script must be omitted after publication. Times out after 90s.

tools.name: find
tools.description: Find by text/label/value/role/id and run action; the action defaults to click. The role locator matches snapshot kind vocabulary (button, text, text-field, switch, ...); pre-reconciliation leaf spellings (statictext, edittext, textview) stay accepted on the nodes that carried them during a deprecation window. The focus and type actions aim at a text field: the match or the field holding it, even beside other fields, or else the one enabled on-screen field inside the match. Several enabled on-screen fields inside the match refuse with AMBIGUOUS_MATCH and the field candidates, and a disabled target refuses with reason target_disabled. Web text boxes are not recognized as text fields. Times out after 90s.

tools.name: fold
tools.description: Fold or unfold a foldable iPhone simulator (iPhone Duo) or a foldable Android emulator into the closed, half-open, or open pose. iOS sends a simulator HID hinge event, then reads the hinge angle back inside the simulator to confirm it, and can follow timestamped angle keyframes; Android sets the emulator console posture, then confirms the device state the guest commits and reports the angle read from the hinge sensor, which can differ from the AVD profile's per-posture angles, and dismisses the lock screen a fold to the cover display can raise. On iOS a pose change moves the app to a different panel with a different point size; on Android a fold to or from closed moves the app between the cover and inner displays, and any pose change can reshape the app window, whose size the next snapshot reports. Either way every ref and coordinate from before it is stale. Taps, long presses, and scrolling target the app window on its current panel in closed, half-open, and open poses. Simulator and emulator only; iOS requires the iOS simulator SDK; Device Hub and host Accessibility permission are not required. An iOS simulator in a scoped simulator set folds the same way as one in the default set. Times out after 255s.

tools.name: hardware-button
tools.description: Press a phone hardware button once: volume-up, volume-down, power, mute, sleep, wake, media-play-pause, media-next, media-previous, media-rewind, or media-fast-forward. The press is dispatched without activating the session app and nothing is re-observed afterwards, so the OS decides what the key does — which audio stream a volume press moves, which media session a media key reaches, and whether the HUD shows, is device behavior this command does not claim. Power toggles the Android screen; sleep and wake are the explicit Android events that turn it off or on without toggling, and after a press that turns it off, later commands may hit a locked screen. Android (ADB-backed and Appium) presses all eleven on phones and tablets; a physical iPhone or iPad presses volume only through the local runner or Appium, never power, mute, sleep, wake, or media. iOS Simulators, Android TV and tvOS targets refuse this command. Times out after 90s.

tools.name: open
tools.description: Boot the selected device when needed, then open an app, deep link, or URL in a session. With a known app, start with open and foreground: a fresh open returns the initial interactive snapshot with refs (or initialSnapshotError: then run snapshot). Do not probe with devices or apps first; list them only for an unknown app id, and never guess one. The app or URL inputs select the foreground automation target. Remote daemons refuse file: URLs in open targets and launch URLs with reason REMOTE_HOST_INPUT_DENIED. Local web content is supported over HTTP(S). metroHost, metroPort, and bundleUrl choose the app's Metro server and save its address for later reloads. launchUrl selects the app's launch URL and does not select the reload server. A fresh open without Metro hints clears an older same-name binding; close also clears it. Times out after 90s; a caller-supplied budget extends it.

tools.name: scroll
tools.description: Scroll in a direction, or toward the top/bottom edge of scrollable content. The until input scrolls to an off-screen selector in one command. The optional amount is the finger-path fraction of the viewport axis, honored up to 0.8 of it; directional scrolls reduce release momentum, while app scroll physics determine the final content offset. A visible keyboard shortens the swiped band instead of being dismissed; when too little is left, the command refuses with scroll_keyboard_occludes_surface. A directional scroll also reports the movement it observed as movement: moved, at-edge, unchanged, or unobserved when the two reads could not back a claim either way; an unchanged surface inside a container that still hides content in that direction refuses with scroll_no_progress rather than repeating the requested distance. The movement field is absent where a tier verifies per pass (top/bottom, until), where the runtime cannot read a screen, where a settle observation or a replay already owns that observation, or where the operator opted out of it. Times out after 90s; a caller-supplied budget extends it.

instructions:
agent-device drives iOS, Android, tvOS, Android TV, macOS, Linux, and web apps. Tools mirror CLI commands of the same name; CLI flags are camelCase properties (--settle -> settle: true). If your client defers tool schemas, load a tool's schema before its first call.

Start: known app -> call open {app, foreground: true} at once; do not probe with devices, apps, appstate, snapshot, or screenshot first. open returns the initial interactive snapshot with @refs. Unknown app id: devices, then apps, then open the discovered id; never invent ids. Existing session: continue from its state, do not reopen.

Loop: back/click/fill/hover/longpress/press/scroll with settle: true; the response is the settled UI diff, continue from it. A known multi-step walk is one batch call: steps [{command, input}]. To reach an off-screen target, scroll {direction, until: "<selector>"} scrolls until it is on screen in one call, and direction "bottom" runs to the end of the content; repeated bare scrolls are the slow way to find something. snapshot {interactiveOnly: true} only when the diff lacks the next target or did not settle. Verify with wait {kind: "text", text}, wait {selector}, wait {absent: selector}, is, or get; a bare screenshot is not verification. find acts and clicks by default; to check only, pass action: "exists". End with close.

Targets are top-level arguments: press {ref: "@e12"}, click {selector: "id=submit"}, press {x, y}. Copy refs byte-for-byte (@e12, @e12~s4; keep @ and any ~sN). Refs go stale after mutations. Prefer refs, then id/label/role selectors; coordinates last. On a sparse/AX-unavailable warning its refs and selectors are invalid: screenshot, read the image, press {x, y}, then snapshot the changed screen.

Errors carry hints; follow them instead of re-planning. Call help only for specialized work (gestures, scripting, TV, macOS, web, remote, debugging) or an unclear command shape, never at startup.
